title: NGC 1512 and NGC 1510
caption: The merging galaxies NGC 1512 and NGC 1510, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: ngc 1510, NGC 1512 · constellation Horologium · about 30 million light-years away (source figure)

recognition.text: Ranked #86 on ESA/Hubble’s published “Top 100 Images” list (an institutional selection, not an audience score).

story: The barred spiral galaxy NGC 1512 sits on the left of this Hubble composite, with the dwarf galaxy NGC 1510 on the right. It was stitched together from two separate Hubble pointings, and both galaxies lie about 30 million light-years from Earth in the constellation Horologium.

The pair are in the middle of merging. When the process is complete, the larger NGC 1512 will have cannibalised its small companion, taking its stars and gas into itself. Mergers in which a big galaxy swallows a much smaller one are one of the ways galaxies grow over time.

A barred spiral like NGC 1512 has a straight band of stars across its center, with its arms extending from the bar's ends. A dwarf galaxy is a small system holding far fewer stars than a large spiral. Hubble has caught the two while they are still separate, before the smaller one disappears into its neighbor.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (7.54 x 2.76 arcminutes) and distance (30 million light years), the frame spans roughly 66,000 × 24,000 light-years. Its light set out about 30 million years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3 observed in ultraviolet, visible and near-infrared light. The color mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: The ultraviolet and near-infrared parts of this light are invisible to the eye.
